title: 12 prompts for boiling animation (frame by frame)
key_takeaways: 'Boiling' animation is faked by generating 12 near-identical stills of the same word and cutting between them on a timeline — the tiny inconsistencies between generations become the wobble.
Every prompt holds the base constant (word 'Flux', Manrope Regular, tight kerning, pure white RGB 255,255,255 background, monochrome dust and fine film grain) and varies only the hand-drawn overlay.

The 12 variations are a deliberate mark-making ladder: clean, graphite underline, ballpoint oval, ink asterisks, red felt-tip strikethrough, broad marker double-underline, pencil scribble-out, red arrow squiggle, square brackets, wavy centerline, signature squiggle, stray ink dots.

Specifying the exact instrument (thin graphite pencil, fine black ballpoint, translucent red felt-tip, broad permanent marker) is what produces believable analog texture instead of a generic 'hand-drawn' filter.
The word 'imperfect' is stated explicitly in the prompts — perfection is what breaks the effect.
Workflow: copy prompt, generate in Flux.2 Max or Nano Banana Pro, drop frames sequentially on an LTX or NLE timeline, cut short, add SFX.
This is a lead-magnet freebie doc gating on a follow, with an LTX Studio referral link on every prompt.

title: How to Build an MCP-Ready Design System
key_takeaways: The reason AI coding agents butcher a UI over MCP is not the MCP server — it is that the design system was authored for human readers, so access is granted without understanding.
Failure mode is specific and recognizable: the agent hallucinates custom CSS, introduces conflicting button variants, and ignores layout tokens.
Invert the traditional order: do NOT build tokens and variables before designing screens. Build raw Figma components with clean props and no variables first.
Design 2-3 high-fidelity, complex screens of the real product first, so the organic design patterns actually exist before you try to name them.

Connect the Figma file over MCP and have the model analyze the finished layouts to extract the token naming convention and scale — the prompt given is to analyze colors, spacing, shadows, borders, and typography across the screens.

The claimed advantage is that the model reads the mathematical relationships already present in real layouts faster than a human can, so the token architecture is derived from product reality rather than guessed in a vacuum.
Author concedes up front that nobody — designers or engineers — yet knows definitively which design-system format LLMs parse best.

title: 50 design prompts from ex-Warner designer (Nano Banana Pro)
key_takeaways: The article is an index, not a tutorial: 50 previously-posted prompts sorted into 8 categories (branded products, brand identity systems, 3D objects, posters & illustrations, icons, mockups, apparel & fashion, typography), each linking back to the original post that holds the full prompt.
The core reusable pattern across every prompt is a single bracketed variable — swap [BRAND NAME] or [CHARACTER NAME] and regenerate; the prompt itself carries the art direction.

The most advanced prompts are agentic rather than descriptive: they instruct the model to infer the brand's real colors, typography, and cultural positioning from training data, and even to pick a plausible collaboration partner on its own (#35 cross-brand sneaker collab, #40 outerwear).
Prompts are written in the voice of a role plus a deliverable ('Act as a graphic design creative director constructing a Campaign Visual Identity Grid'), not as a list of adjectives.

Post-generation polish is treated as mandatory, with a named toolchain: upscale via Magnific.ai / LetsEnhance.io / Topaz Gigapixel AI, cut background via remove.bg, then final layout, text and spacing in Figma or Photoshop before export.
Structural prompt sections are capitalized and delimited (COMPOSITION, CONTENT SCOPE, PHASE) so the model treats them as separate constraints rather than prose.
Distribution strategy is visible in the numbers: the catalog article aggregates link equity from ~50 individual posts and drives to a single gated product page.

title: How I built Gucci x Crocs campaign from 1 image + GPT-v2
key_takeaways: The central move is 'image-to-engine': never copy a reference image, extract its underlying creative system (core tension, color/material language, typography direction, composition logic, signature visual device, grid) into a brand board, then rebuild a different brand on top of that system.
Prompt 1 explicitly instructs 'Do NOT copy the reference directly' — the deconstruction step is what makes the output original rather than derivative.

The 5-prompt sequence is fixed and each stage locks a decision: 1) deconstruct reference into a 4:3 brand board, 2) re-skin the system onto your brand, 3) generate an asset moodboard, 4) write the brief/idea/goals slide, 5) produce the hero key visual.

Layout guardrails are written into the prompt rather than fixed later: no overlapping text on active backgrounds, clean margins, consistent spacing, clear modular grid, minimal micro-copy, no overcrowding.
A concrete refinement lever: 'make 30% less images, but make them tighter and looking more like a bento grid' — asking for fewer, denser tiles beats asking for better ones.
Known failure mode of GPT image 2 called out directly: it overlays text on models' faces, which requires a separate patch prompt.
Locking the vision in a brief slide (brief + idea + goals) is treated as an input to the AI as much as a client deliverable — it re-grounds later generations.
Key visual prompts should name the publication-level bar ('deserves to be on the first page of Forbes or Esquire') instead of listing style adjectives.
Author's stated prerequisite: learn traditional creative-direction and marketing frameworks first, because AI amplifies that judgment rather than replacing it.

title: How to Name Your Company: The Complete Playbook
key_takeaways: Aim for the 'tension zone' (half the team loves it, half hates it) over the 'invisible zone' (everyone says 'that's fine') — Andy Grove approved Pentium precisely because it was polarizing, which means it has energy.

Never name after what the product does; climb the benefit ladder feature → functional → emotional → ultimate, and name from the top rung (a PM tool's ultimate benefit is 'clarity', not 'project management').
The first and most important decision is what you are NOT: map 20 competitors, identify the dominant naming patterns in the category, and rule them off-limits.
Generate far more candidates than feels reasonable — target 300+ minimum (agencies run 2,000+); most founders fail by picking the least offensive of 50.

Sound carries meaning: hard consonants (K, T, P) read strong and precise, soft sounds (L, M, S) read smooth; V is the most daring letter — Vercel was built from versatile + accelerate + excel to replace the unspellable Zeit.
Test by asking 10-15 people one-on-one 'what does this make you feel?' — never 'do you like it?' — and avoid focus groups, which optimize for consensus and push you into invisibility.
Score finalists on distinctiveness, processing fluency, emotional resonance, energy and longevity, but pick the 9-10 on distinctiveness and energy over the balanced all-7s: remarkable beats balanced.
Renaming pre-Series B is cheap and generates PR energy; the claim is no marketplace evidence exists for losing 'name equity', and the real risk is a decade of daily friction.

AI has shifted the advantage from generation to judgment — it produces 200-300 candidates in minutes but cannot sense energy or tension, and first-pass output is bland without the earlier strategy phases.
Practical constraints: 1-3 syllables (2 ideal), invented words must obey the target language's phonetic rules, and .com matters less than a decade ago but still matters in B2B.
